title: The Danger of a French Right Turn for Ukraine
author: Ian Bremmer
body:
As France moves toward its two-round presidential election next spring, President Vladimir Putin of Russia and President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine will be watching closely. Both understand that a victory for the current frontrunner, Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right National Rally party, could be Putin’s biggest political windfall since he ordered the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

A Le Pen victory is far from assured. This will be her fourth run for president; her father ran five times before her. Her second-round opponent can count on support from millions of voters who consider a Le Pen presidency unacceptable.

But as peaceful protests across France over high prices and rough conditions in schools have given way to rioting and looting in recent weeks, President Emmanuel Macron and his centrist coalition have lost much of their remaining popularity. Their decline also threatens the prospects of Edouard Philippe, the presidential candidate of the center-right Horizons party, the centrist most likely to succeed the term-limited Macron.

Recent polls put Le Pen’s support at about 38%, compared with just 14% for Philippe. The election is still six months away, and Philippe could gain support if voters opposed to Le Pen see him as the strongest alternative. Yet all recent surveys show Le Pen leading him by high single-digits in a head-to-head contest.

If Le Pen wins, she is likely to halt France’s bilateral aid to Ukraine beginning in 2028. She could also block Europe’s financial support for Ukraine by withholding France’s contribution to the European Union budget. And she is likely to oppose using frozen Russian assets to fund Ukraine’s defense.

The consequences would extend well beyond France. If a President Le Pen blocked E.U. support for Kyiv, European aid would have to flow through individual nations. Several European governments—Italy, Spain, Greece, Austria, Hungary, Slovakia and others less committed to Ukraine’s defense—might well follow France’s lead and give priority to their national budgets. Kyiv’s more steadfast European allies could not fill the gap by themselves, and the Trump Administration won’t make up the difference.

A Le Pen victory could also boost Russia’s economy. For nearly a decade, she has called for lifting E.U. sanctions on Russia. The next renewal vote is set for July, just two months after she would take office, and she would have veto power. But the threat a Le Pen presidency poses to Ukraine extends well beyond money. To join the European Union, Kyiv needs unanimous support from all current members. Membership is already a difficult proposition, for reasons both political and practical. A Le Pen veto would close off that prospect for as long as she remains in power.

Losing that prospect would also make it harder for Zelensky to offer territorial and other concessions in negotiations to end the fighting. With no opportunity of either E.U. membership or a security guarantee against future Russian aggression, any deal he asks Ukrainians to accept would feel more like surrender. With Le Pen crippling European backing for Kyiv while boosting Russia’s ability to continue the war, Europe would have little leverage left to press Putin for a deal or to advance alternatives to plans put forward by President Donald Trump and his envoys.

For the moment, Zelensky has more immediate challenges. He must steady relations with the ever-erratic American president, prepare his country for another cold winter of Russian missile and drone attacks, and navigate a complex political situation at home. But if Le Pen is elected president of France next May, Zelensky will have to begin courting her immediately. It won’t be easy. Le Pen will arrive with her own priorities: addressing France’s many economic and social problems, remaking her country’s relations with the EU, and delivering on promises to reduce state spending on foreign policy.

Since the Russian invasion, Zelensky has worked relentlessly to secure and sustain support abroad. A Le Pen presidency could prove his biggest challenge yet.
